props.title: The Holy Mountain

sections.content: The Holy Mountain stands as Alejandro Jodorowsky's masterpiece of surrealist cinema, pushing boundaries far beyond his earlier El Topo (1970). The film blends mystical symbolism, religious iconography, and biting social satire into a psychedelic journey that influenced generations of filmmakers. Its meticulous production design and shocking imagery established new possibilities for avant-garde cinema, laying groundwork for later works like Eraserhead (1977) and Enter the Void (2009).

sections.content: Jodorowsky's attention to symbolic detail is unmatched - every frame contains layers of alchemical, Tarot, and religious imagery carefully arranged to create maximum impact. The film's infamous production involved real spiritual practices, with cast members living communally and engaging in actual mystical exercises. This dedication to authenticity shows in the raw energy of performances, particularly in the alchemical transformation sequences that influenced later psychedelic films like Beyond the Black Rainbow (2010).

The film's critique of organized religion and capitalism remains razor-sharp today. Jodorowsky's portrayal of religious corruption through grotesque imagery predates similar themes in films like The Devils (1971) and Mother! (2017). His use of shocking juxtaposition and body horror would later influence directors like David Cronenberg and Gaspar Noé. SUBHEAD: Visual Innovation and Cultural Impact

sections.content: The film's groundbreaking visual style combines elaborate set pieces with guerrilla filmmaking techniques. Scenes like the Conquest of Mexico reenactment with chameleons and toads remain unmatched in their bizarre creativity. This blend of high art and low-budget ingenuity influenced midnight movie culture and experimental filmmakers like Matthew Barney's Cremaster Cycle (1994-2002) and Kenneth Anger's later works.

While The Holy Mountain was initially met with controversy and limited distribution, its influence has grown exponentially. Modern filmmakers like Panos Cosmatos and Ari Aster have cited it as a major inspiration, with films like Mandy (2018) and Midsommar (2019) carrying forward its tradition of visually striking spiritual horror.
